title: What is Rust used for?

spans.text: LESSON PURPOSE

Goal: apply “What is Rust used for?” to a real program or device. The key principle is: Rust combines high-level abstractions and low-level control with compile-time checks. In a project, follow this guidance: Rust does not require a garbage collector, but resource management still needs design: reason about ownership, lifetimes, and failures.
QUESTION: What will this example do? Predict the result first.
EXAMPLE CODE

spans.code:
fn parse_port(text: &str) -> Result<u16, std::num::ParseIntError> { Ok(text.parse()?) }
fn main() { println!("{:?}", parse_port("8080")); }

spans.text: EXPECTED RESULT
CORE EXPLANATION

Rust is a systems language for software that needs performance, low-level resource control, and strong memory safety. It is used for operating-system components, command-line tools, network services, game infrastructure, WebAssembly, and microcontroller firmware. Ownership and the borrow checker catch many memory errors at compile time, while requiring developers to model ownership, borrowing, and types explicitly.

Company examples: Google uses Rust in the Android platform; AWS's Firecracker virtual-machine monitor and Cloudflare's Pingora proxy are Rust projects. This does not mean all of those companies' software is written in Rust; they choose it for suitable system components. Sources: https://source.android.com/docs/setup/build/rust/building-rust-modules · https://github.com/firecracker-microvm/firecracker · https://github.com/cloudflare/pingora
IMPORTANT LINE BREAKDOWN

Key line: `fn parse_port(text: &str) -> Result<u16, std::num::ParseIntError> { Ok(text.parse()?) }`
What it does: Rust combines high-level abstractions and low-level control with compile-time checks.
Why it is used: Rust does not require a garbage collector, but resource management still needs design: reason about ownership, lifetimes, and failures.
If omitted or changed: Match the language's strengths to latency, memory budget, target platform, and team experience.
